title: Banking & NI Act
sub: Law of Banking & Negotiable Instruments · BR Act 1949 · NI Act 1881 · SARFAESI 2002 · Osmania LLB (3 YDC) Sem V
journey: Money enters a regulated bank, a customer opens an account, writes instruments that travel by endorsement, the paying and collecting banks move the money — and when a loan goes bad, the bank uses its lien, its securities and the DRT.

stations.name: Bank & banking
stations.one: Accepting public deposits for lending, repayable on demand, withdrawable by cheque.

stations.name: History & nationalisation
stations.one: Indigenous bankers → Presidency banks → SBI → 14 banks nationalised (1969) + 6 (1980).
stations.boss: R.C. Cooper v Union of India (1970)

stations.name: BR Act — features
stations.one: Licence, capital, CRR / SLR, management, control of advances, inspection, nomination.

stations.name: Reserve Bank of India
stations.one: Issues currency, banks for Govt and banks, lender of last resort, controls credit, regulates.

stations.name: Kinds of banks
stations.one: Commercial, co-operative, development (NABARD, IDBI), mixed, group, universal, payments.

stations.name: Banking & IT
stations.one: Core banking, UPI, e-cheques and truncated cheques, valid under the IT Act.

stations.name: Licence, ombudsman, liquidity
stations.one: No banking without an RBI licence (appeal 30 days); RBI Ombudsman; liquidity ratios.

stations.name: Who is a customer?
stations.one: One who has an account and banking dealings — duration doesn’t matter.
stations.boss: Great Western Rly v London & County Bank (1901)

stations.name: Debtor & creditor
stations.one: Your deposit becomes the bank’s money; it owes you on demand.
stations.boss: Foley v Hill (1848) — banker is debtor, not trustee

stations.name: Trustee & fiduciary
stations.one: Money for a specific purpose is held in trust; the bank owes trust and confidence.
stations.boss: Woods v Martins Bank (1959) — liable for negligent advice

stations.name: Bailee & locker
stations.one: Safe custody makes the bank a bailee (care of a prudent man); a locker makes it a lessor.
stations.boss: Amitabha Dasgupta v United Bank of India (2021)

stations.name: Agent
stations.one: Collecting cheques and following standing instructions, the bank is the customer’s agent.

stations.name: Duty to honour
stations.one: Funds available → must pay; wrongful dishonour → damages (trader more than non-trader).
stations.boss: Gibbons v Westminster Bank (1939)

stations.name: Secrecy
stations.one: Keep accounts secret — except law, public duty, bank’s interest, consent.
stations.boss: Tournier v National Provincial Bank (1924)

stations.name: Garnishee order
stations.one: A court order freezing the judgment-debtor’s money in his sole name.
stations.hook: Freeze only what is his alone

stations.name: Negotiable instrument
stations.one: Note, bill or cheque, payable to order or bearer — passes like money; HDC gets clean title.

stations.name: Promissory note
stations.one: Unconditional, signed promise to pay a certain sum to a certain person.

stations.name: Bill of exchange
stations.one: Unconditional, signed order to pay; three parties; acceptance.

stations.name: Cheque & its kinds
stations.one: A bill on a banker, payable on demand — bearer, order, crossed, post-dated, stale, electronic.
stations.hook: Bill on a bank, on demand

stations.name: Drafts, warrants & TCs
stations.one: Banker’s drafts, dividend warrants, traveller’s cheques; money & postal orders are not NIs.

stations.name: Crossing
stations.one: Two parallel lines — pay only through a bank; special, not negotiable, account payee.
stations.boss: Indian Overseas Bank v Industrial Chain Concern (1990)

stations.name: Presumptions
stations.one: Consideration, date, order of endorsements, HDC — all presumed till disproved.
stations.boss: Rangappa v Sri Mohan (2010) — S.139 covers the debt

stations.name: Maturity & grace
stations.one: 3 days of grace for time instruments; holiday → preceding day; words beat figures.

stations.name: Holder & HDC
stations.one: Holder in due course: for value, before maturity, in good faith — gets a better title.

stations.name: Endorsement
stations.one: Signature for negotiation — blank (bearer) or full (to order); restrictive stops it.
stations.hook: Bearer by delivery · order by endorsement

stations.name: Conditional & partial
stations.one: Conditional endorsement waits for the event; endorsement for part of the amount is invalid.

stations.name: Forgery & fraud
stations.one: A forged endorsement passes no title; theft, fraud or duress don’t hurt an HDC.
stations.hook: Forgery kills title · fraud spares the HDC

stations.name: Liability & discharge
stations.one: Maker / acceptor primary; drawer / endorsers on notice; discharge by payment, release, delay.

stations.name: Dishonour, noting, protest
stations.one: Not accepted or not paid → notice to all parties; notary notes and protests (foreign bills must).

stations.name: Material alteration
stations.one: An unauthorised material change voids the instrument against non-consenting parties.
stations.boss: Koch v Dicks (1933) — place of drawing is material
stations.hook: Change the deal, lose the party

stations.name: Cheque bounce — S.138
stations.one: Notice in 30 days, 15 days to pay, complaint in 1 month; 20% interim compensation.
stations.boss: Dashrath Rupsingh Rathod v Maharashtra (2014)

stations.name: Paying banker
stations.one: The drawee bank: checks form, date, signature, funds, crossing, stop orders before paying.

stations.name: Payment in due course
stations.one: As per apparent tenor, in good faith, without negligence, to the person in possession.

stations.name: Statutory protection
stations.one: Forged endorsement (S.85), drafts (85A), crossed cheques (128), invisible alteration (89).

stations.name: Forged signature
stations.one: No mandate, no protection — the bank bears the loss.
stations.boss: Canara Bank v Canara Sales Corp (1987)

stations.name: Countermand
stations.one: Stop payment binds the bank only when it actually receives it.
stations.boss: Curtice v London City & Midland Bank (1908)

stations.name: Collecting banker
stations.one: Collects for its customer; S.131 shields it if in good faith and without negligence.
stations.boss: Lloyds Bank v Savory (1933) — negligence defeats protection

stations.name: Banker’s lien
stations.one: Keeps the customer’s securities for any balance due; can sell after notice; not safe custody.
stations.boss: Brandao v Barnett (1846) — lien is part of the law merchant

stations.name: Set-off
stations.one: Combine the same customer’s accounts — same right, debt due and certain.
stations.boss: Garnett v McKewan (1872)

stations.name: Lending principles
stations.one: Safety, liquidity, profitability, purpose, security, spread, national interest.

stations.name: Securities
stations.one: Pledge goods, mortgage land, assign life policies, pledge shares, documents of title.
stations.hook: Goods: pledge · Land: mortgage · Policy: assign

stations.name: Guarantor
stations.one: Surety pays if the debtor doesn’t; liability co-extensive and immediate.
stations.boss: Bank of Bihar v Damodar Prasad (1969)

stations.name: Bank guarantee
stations.one: Bank’s independent promise to pay on demand; courts stop it only for fraud or irretrievable harm.
stations.boss: U.P. State Sugar Corp v Sumac (1997)

stations.name: Letter of credit
stations.one: Bank pays the seller against the right documents; strict compliance; UCP 600.
stations.boss: Equitable Trust Co v Dawson Partners (1927)

stations.name: DRT & SARFAESI
stations.one: DRT decides bank claims of ₹20 lakh+; SARFAESI lets banks seize NPAs’ security after 60-day notice.
stations.boss: Mardia Chemicals v Union of India (2004)

xfer: no lien on safe-custody articles or locker contents
forged endorsement v forged signature — opposite results
crossed cheques are collected through a bank — S.131
bank’s wrongful dishonour v drawer’s S.138 crime
debtor–creditor balances can be set off

routes.title: Does the holder get a good title?
steps: Is there a forged endorsement in the chain of an order instrument?
yes
No title passes through a forgery — the true owner recovers (nemo dat).
Did he take it for value, before maturity, in good faith?
no
Only a holder — takes subject to defects; a gift-holder can’t enforce against the drawer (S.43).
Does he claim from an HDC but was himself party to the fraud?
yes
No — S.53 protects only those not party to the fraud.
routes.end: Good title as a holder in due course — even if it was lost, stolen or obtained by fraud earlier (S.9, 53, 58) ✓

routes.title: Is the paying banker protected?
steps: Was the drawer’s signature forged?
yes
No mandate, no protection — the bank bears the loss (Canara Bank).
Did a countermand or notice of death reach the bank before payment?
yes
Bank can’t debit the customer (S.31; Curtice).
Was the payment in due course — apparent tenor, good faith, no negligence (S.10)?
no
Protection lost — bank liable.
routes.end: Protected: forged endorsement (S.85(1)), bearer (85(2)), draft (85A), crossing (128), invisible alteration (89) ✓

routes.title: Lien, set-off — or nothing?
steps: Was it given for safe custody, a locker, or a specific purpose / trust?
yes
No lien — the bank is only bailee / lessor / trustee.
Is it money in another account of the same customer, in the same right?
yes
Set-off (combine accounts) if the debt is due and certain.
Is the customer’s debt actually due?
no
Wait — no lien for a contingent or future debt.
routes.end: General lien (Contract Act S.171) — an implied pledge: may sell after reasonable notice ✓

routes.title: Cheque bounced — can I prosecute?
steps: Was it given for a legally enforceable debt or liability?
no
No S.138 — e.g. a gift; the S.139 presumption is rebutted.
Presented within 3 months and returned for insufficient funds, exceeding arrangement, stop payment or closed account?
no
Not S.138 — e.g. bank failure: sue on the debt.
Notice sent within 30 days and still unpaid 15 days after receipt?
no
Send notice within 30 days of the return memo and wait 15 days first.
routes.end: Complaint within 1 month before the JMFC where the payee’s bank is (S.138, 142); seek 20% interim compensation (S.143A) ✓

routes.title: The endorsement looks odd
steps: Is it for only part of the amount?
yes
Not a negotiation (S.56) — unless the rest was already paid.
Does it depend on an event (“if he returns from Paris”)?
yes
Conditional (S.52): the endorsee can’t claim until it happens.
Does it say “pay C only” or “for collection”?
yes
Restrictive (S.50): no further negotiation.
Blank first, then full, then passed without endorsement?
yes
S.55: the last holder can sue the drawer and the blank endorser, not the full endorser.
routes.end: Valid negotiation — the endorsee becomes the holder (S.14–16, 50) ✓

routes.title: Must the bank reveal or freeze the account?
steps: Is there a court garnishee order?
yes
Freeze only the debtor’s own-name balance — not joint, trust or estate accounts; set off own dues first.
Does a law demand it (Income-tax S.133(6), court order, PMLA)?
yes
Disclose only what is asked — compulsion of law (Tournier).
Public duty, the bank’s own interest, or the customer’s consent?
yes
Disclosure allowed (Tournier exceptions).
routes.end: Keep it secret — wrongful disclosure is a breach of contract and privacy ✗
